question: How does the convergence rate of classical Monte Carlo integration scale with increasing dimension d?
options: It decreases exponentially with dimension d
It remains constant at O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of d
It improves quadratically through more dimensions
The curse of dimensionality is completely bypassed
explanation: Exactly that is the magic of Monte Carlo! No matter if 2 or 100 dimensions, the convergence rate remains at O(1/sqrt(N)). That's why we love MC in high dimensions. Stay tuned!

question: Why does JAX not have a global random state like numpy.random?
options: To prevent race conditions on parallelized GPUs/TPUs
Because functional purity (Pure Functions) is enforced
Because Google wants to keep the mathematical constant Pi secret
JAX developers simply forgot to implement it
explanation: JAX forces us into functional purity. A global state would lead to nasty race conditions during parallel calculations on GPUs/TPUs. Clean code pays off!

question: What happens if you reuse a JAX PRNGKey in a loop without splitting it?
options: The code immediately aborts with a compiler error
Exactly identical random numbers are generated every time
The simulation loses its functional purity
The system secretly switches to memory mode
explanation: Watch out, trap! Since JAX is functionally pure, the same key always delivers the same output. So never forget your jax.random.split(), otherwise you'll simulate Groundhog Day!

question: Which property fundamentally defines a first-order discrete Markov chain?
options: The system has no memory of historical states
The future depends exclusively on the current state
Transition probabilities must always remain absolutely stable
It was originally invented for the analysis of quanta
explanation: This is the famous Markov property (memorylessness). The chain is not interested in the past, but only in the here and now. Keep it simple!

question: What does Value-at-Risk (VaR_95%) describe in a stochastic business simulation?
options: The maximum profit that the company will achieve to 95%
The loss limit that occurs in the worst 5% of cases
The exact mean of all simulated revenue paths
The statistical risk that the GPU will melt due to overheating
explanation: VaR is your risk radar! At 95% confidence, it shows you the loss that is only exceeded in the worst 5% of scenarios. A must-know for risk management!

question: Which JAX primitive transforms a single-key simulation into a massively parallel vectorized execution?
options: jax.jit
jax.vmap
jax.lax.scan
jax.grad
explanation: vmap (vectorizing map) is your best friend for performance! It takes a function for a single input and runs it parallel across entire batches. Mega efficient!

question: Why is a log-normal distribution often used for operational costs in Monte Carlo models?
options: Because costs can never be negative
To model rare, extremely high loss risks (fat-tails)
Because it is more symmetrical than the classic Gaussian distribution
So that the axes in the plot look nicer
explanation: Costs cannot be negative and often have outliers upwards (fat-tails). The log-normal distribution models this asymmetric risk perfectly. Well thought out!

question: How does a structural Black Swan event mathematically affect a Markov model?
options: The transition matrix P(t) is modified time-dependently and transiently
Probabilities shift abruptly into crisis states
The system breaks down deterministically and stops
All probabilities instantaneously become perfectly equal
explanation: Black Swans break the normal rules. Mathematically, this means that our transition probabilities change abruptly and jump into crisis states. Expect the unexpected!

question: How do Antigravity 2.0 Skills and Gemini 3.5 Flash support the stochastic pipeline?
options: Through automated profiling of JAX compilation times
Autonomous subagents test code variation limits in the sandbox terminal
They completely prohibit the use of random numbers
They replace mathematical formulas with pure AI hallucinations
